flashcards.q: What is the full IAM policy evaluation order, outermost to innermost?
flashcards.a: Explicit deny (any layer) wins immediately > SCP > RCP > resource-based policy > permissions boundary > session policy > identity-based policy > default deny if nothing explicitly allowed.

flashcards.q: Do SCPs, RCPs, and permissions boundaries ever grant permissions by themselves?
flashcards.a: No. They are ceilings evaluated as an intersection with identity/resource policies — they can only take away, never grant. Only identity-based policies (or resource-based policies for same-account/cross-account grants) actually allow anything.

flashcards.q: What does cross-account S3 access require, on which sides?
flashcards.a: Both sides must explicitly allow: the resource-owning account's bucket policy must grant the calling account's principal, AND the calling account's own identity policy on that principal must also allow the action on that resource ARN.

flashcards.q: What problem does sts:ExternalId in a trust policy solve?
flashcards.a: The confused deputy problem: a third-party vendor with AssumeRole access into many customer accounts could act on the wrong customer's behalf. ExternalId is a per-customer secret the vendor must supply on every AssumeRole call, preventing accidental cross-tenant misrouting.

flashcards.q: What fraction of vendors were found to implement sts:ExternalId incorrectly, per NCC Group research?
flashcards.a: 37% did not implement it correctly at all, and another 15% implemented it in the UI but never validated it server-side.

flashcards.q: IRSA vs EKS Pod Identity: what's the mechanical difference?
flashcards.a: IRSA (2019) uses a per-cluster OIDC trust policy on the IAM role plus a webhook that injects a projected token, exchanged via AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Pod Identity (GA 2023) uses an EKS Auth API and a Pod Identity Agent DaemonSet; the trust relationship lives in EKS's control plane, so one role is portable across clusters without editing its trust policy.

flashcards.q: Why is iam:PassRole a quiet privilege-escalation path?
flashcards.a: PassRole grants the right to attach a role to a service resource (Lambda, EC2, ECS) without granting that role's permissions directly. A user with PassRole on an admin role plus the ability to create a Lambda can run arbitrary code with admin permissions, bypassing their own narrower identity policy entirely.

flashcards.q: How should iam:PassRole be scoped to prevent escalation?
flashcards.a: Never Resource:"*". Scope Resource to specific role ARNs or a naming pattern, and add a Condition on iam:PassedToService restricting which AWS service the role can be passed to.

flashcards.q: Difference between aws:SourceArn, aws:SourceAccount, and aws:PrincipalOrgID?
flashcards.a: SourceArn restricts to exactly one resource (strongest, best for confused-deputy prevention). SourceAccount restricts to any resource in a given account (looser). PrincipalOrgID restricts by which AWS Organization the calling principal belongs to, independent of account, used for org-wide perimeters.

flashcards.q: What are permissions boundaries actually for, in a real org?
flashcards.a: Delegated IAM administration: letting app teams self-service create their own roles via CI while capping what those roles can ever become, without central security reviewing every PR. The effective permission is the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary.

flashcards.q: What gap do Resource Control Policies (RCPs, GA Nov 2024) close that SCPs cannot?
flashcards.a: SCPs only bound identity policies of principals inside the org. RCPs bound what a resource-based policy can grant, including grants to principals OUTSIDE the org — something SCPs are structurally unable to restrict since they don't apply to external principals.

flashcards.q: What is IAM Access Analyzer's unused-access finding, and what's its key limitation?
flashcards.a: A heuristic based on observed CloudTrail activity over a lookback window that flags rarely-used identity permissions as candidates for removal. It can falsely flag genuinely-needed but rarely-exercised permissions (e.g., an annual DR runbook action) and cannot detect a permission used exactly once maliciously.

flashcards.q: What is the default and max duration for STS AssumeRole temporary credentials?
flashcards.a: Default 1 hour; configurable 15 minutes to 12 hours via DurationSeconds on the call, hard-capped by the role's own MaxSessionDuration setting.

flashcards.q: What's the correct first debugging step when a request returns AccessDenied unexpectedly?
flashcards.a: Run aws sts get-caller-identity to confirm which principal is actually making the call — using the wrong profile or an unexpectedly assumed role is the single most common self-inflicted cause of confusing denials.

flashcards.q: Can a resource-based policy alone satisfy a same-account access request without any identity-policy statement?
flashcards.a: Yes. For a same-account principal, an explicit allow in the resource policy (e.g., an S3 bucket policy naming that role's ARN) is sufficient on its own — this differs from cross-account access, which needs both sides to explicitly allow.
